deep.reconstruction:
Context. On the previous folio Gauss studies residues modulo a Gaussian prime pi = a+bi of norm p = a^2+b^2. The worked example there is p = 41 = 5^2+4^2. He tries to attach 'exponents' mu+nu*k to Gaussian integers. On this page he restates the idea as a 'logarithm' (index) theory for the numbers x+bi modulo pi, in a form analogous to ordinary indices.

Text: 'To have the "logarithms" of the numbers x+bi in a similar form, one must introduce a double base.'

1. Setup. Let g be a primitive root mod p. Since Z[i]/(pi) is the field F_p, g is also a primitive root mod pi, so (Z[i]/pi)^* = <g> has order p-1.

2. Two bases. After striking out a first attempt, Gauss sets
   M == g^(p-1-b), which is g^(-b);
   N == g^a (mod pi).

3. First relation. M^a N^b == g^(a(p-1-b)+ab) = g^(a(p-1)) == 1.
   [My remark: this holds identically, because M^a N^b = g^(-ab+ab).] It corresponds to the exponent pair (mu,nu) = (a,b), i.e. mu+nu*i = pi == 0. That is the motivation for the next step.

4. Proposed definition. If L == M^mu N^nu (mod pi), then one should set log L == mu+nu*i (mod pi). The exponents are thus read as a Gaussian integer and reduced mod pi.

5. Closing remark: 'Die ZWEIHEIT muss immer die Hauptsache bleiben' ('the twoness/duality must always remain the main thing').

What the construction really gives [my analysis]:
- M^mu N^nu = g^(a*nu - b*mu).
- a*nu - b*mu is the imaginary part of conj(pi)*(mu+nu*i).
- So the true kernel of (mu,nu) -> M^mu N^nu is the index-(p-1) sublattice {a*nu - b*mu == 0 mod p-1}. This is not an ideal of Z[i].
- The lattice pi*Z[i] has index p, so the proposed logarithm 'mod pi' is not well defined.

The note is an exploratory idea for a two-component ('complex') index calculus. It belongs with his biquadratic-residue researches; the next folio is headed 'Theorie des biquadratischen Rests'.
errors: The definition log L == mu+nu*i (mod pi) is not consistent. M^mu N^nu = g^(a*nu-b*mu) depends only on a*nu-b*mu mod (p-1), not on mu+nu*i mod pi.
Counterexample 1 (p=41, pi=5+4i, g=6): (mu,nu)=(-4,5) corresponds to i*pi == 0 mod pi, yet M^-4 N^5 == g^1 = 6, not 1.
Counterexample 2: (mu,nu)=(p-1,0) gives M^(p-1) = 1, but p-1 == -1, not 0, mod pi.
Structural obstruction: (Z[i]/pi)^* has order p-1 while Z[i]/pi has p elements. No bijective homomorphic 'logarithm' with values in Z[i]/pi can exist; the right target would be a group of order p-1.

The identity M^a N^b == 1 is trivially true (exponent -ab+ab); the 'p-1' in M's exponent only makes it positive. It does not by itself justify the claim that pi is in the kernel in any ideal-theoretic sense.
The same p versus p-1 slip appears on the previous page ('5 log h + 4 log H durch 41', where 40 is what is actually needed).

results.what: Representation of the units mod a Gaussian prime pi=a+bi as M^mu N^nu with M=g^(-b), N=g^a. The exponent pair is to be read as a Gaussian integer mu+nu*i mod pi, i.e. a 'double base' index/logarithm.
results.modern_name: Discrete logarithm (index) modulo a Gaussian prime; an attempted two-dimensional / Z[i]-valued index
results.usually_credited_to: Indices mod p: Gauss (Disquisitiones, 1801) and Jacobi (Canon Arithmeticus, 1839). Indices in Gaussian integers appear in Gauss's biquadratic-residue work (1828/1832) and in Jacobi and Eisenstein.

results.what: Relation M^a N^b == 1 mod pi for the two bases
results.modern_name: Trivial exponent identity; the kernel lattice of (mu,nu) -> g^(a*nu-b*mu)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a short exploratory note on indices modulo Gaussian primes, squarely within Gauss's known biquadratic-residue program. The proposed 'complex logarithm mod pi' does not actually work as stated. There is no new theorem here, only an interesting glimpse of his attempt at a two-component index notion and his remark on 'Zweiheit'.

checkable.asserts: Under Z[i]/(5+4i) = F_41 we have i -> 9, and pi = 5+4i maps to 0.
Counterexample: (mu,nu)=(-4,5), i.e. i*pi == 0 mod pi, gives M^mu N^nu == g, not 1. So log mod pi is not well defined.
(mu,nu)=(p-1,0) gives 1, but p-1 is not == 0 mod pi (it is == -1).
The exponent of g in M^mu N^nu, namely a*nu - b*mu, equals Im(conj(pi)*(mu+nu*i)) for real a,b,mu,nu.
